title: His play
hook: all happens within His will and His play

segments.voice: Yesterday, karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes; your line was he is the doer. Today, the first stanza of ashtpadi eleven.

Rain on the morning of the wedding. A flight canceled. The diagnosis nobody wanted. A baby who arrives three weeks early, on the one day everyone was away. Every life has moments when the plan simply doesn't happen, and nothing you could have done would have changed it. Some people rage. Some go numb. In a Sikh home, an elder may say a short phrase, quietly, sometimes through tears: bhaana mannana. Accept the will. It isn't giving up. It's something harder.
screen: `RAIN ON THE WEDDING DAY.` → `NOTHING YOU COULD HAVE DONE.` → `BHAANA MANNANA: ACCEPT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins: God is able to do, and to have things done. Then: jo tis bhaavai soee hog. Whatever pleases Him comes to pass. Bhaavai and bhaana are one family of words: what pleases God, and so, the will. Then the pictures come fast. In an instant He sets up and takes down. By His order He holds the earth up with no support beneath it. By His order things are born, and by His order they merge back. High and low, every shade and form. He makes and makes, and beholds His own greatness; Nanak, He is pervading all. You might picture a stern ruler issuing commands. But later in Sukhmani, Guru Arjan uses a gentler word for the whole show: khel, play. God makes His own play, the hymn says, and watches it. Picture a child building a sandcastle, delighting in it, letting the tide take it, and building again. Put the will and the play together and you reach the heart of bhaana mannana. For Sikhs, accepting the will isn't accepting that someone up there is cruel. It's trusting that even the rain on the wedding day is inside the play, though no one can see the whole stage. And Sikhs who accept the bhaana still grieve, still fight injustice, still call the doctor. Acceptance is for what you can't change.
screen: `JO TIS BHAAVAI: WHATEVER PLEASES HIM.` · `SET UP AND TAKEN DOWN IN AN INSTANT.` · `KHEL: CREATION AS PLAY.` · `ACCEPTANCE, NOT GIVING UP.` · then, large: `HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: Find one thing that's truly fixed, not something you can still work on: the weather, a past event, someone else's choice, a loss. Notice where you push against it in your body, the jaw, the stomach, the shoulders, and breathe into that place; you don't have to like it, only let it be what it is, inside the play. If you pray, you can say the two words Sikhs use: bhaana mannana.
His play. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and the whole creation is His play, made and watched by its Maker.
Your line: his will. Not giving up, but trusting the play, even on a rainy day. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of 'bhaana mannana', accepting God's will, especially in grief or hardship, while still working to change what can be changed.

chat.says: My aunt said 'bhaana mannana' at the funeral. Does that mean just give up?
options: No. It's accepting what can't be changed as inside God's play, while still grieving and acting.
Yes. If it's God's will, there's no point grieving, seeing a doctor or fighting injustice.
It means pretending the loss didn't hurt, and never speaking about it again.
